# MPL_62_002-050 — Research notes

## Scope and evidential status

These notes concern the 46 retained scans of cote 62: 002, 004–017, 019–026, and 028–050. The transcription, including all reused typescripts, drawings, cancellations, insertions, and margins, was visually read and audited by the primary transcriber; the research comparisons below began only after the 47 TeX files were frozen. The freeze and context-opening events were recorded sequentially at 18:57:54 UTC on 16 November 2026; the combined transcription's SHA-256 is 9d5b838824b3bf4663823f19a80d2c98330181407538c2af34143a0b6f2c6869.

The distinction between evidence and inference is maintained throughout. A manuscript assertion is not certified merely by being transcribed; an earlier working note is a claim unless checked; a result-register entry retains exactly its supplied review status. No source reading was changed after the context opened, and every proposed correction or qualification below belongs only to these notes. The primary transcriber wrote and checked the final notes; research assistants compared frozen text and literature only, without reading or auditing the manuscript images.

The most consequential mathematical checks concern the changing j normalization, the arithmetic and infinitesimal qualifications to the special-invariant classifications, the full étaleness condition in reconstruction over a normal base, and missing or ambiguous hypotheses in the reused algebra text. The two requested witness questions receive bounded negative answers in Q01–Q02. These findings do not assert an exhaustive archive search or historical priority.

The context comparison beneath each note states whether the manuscript adds to, restates, differs from, or fails to match the prior material. Lexical absence alone is not treated as proof of mathematical absence: the closest substantive passages and the earlier dossier's overall subject were also compared. Search hits for a different kind of discriminant, a TikZ path called “cycle”, or a repeated theorem number were not treated as subject matches.

The note paragraphs are deliberately limited to one to four sentences per item. “Own idea” means an editorial deduction, example, or proposed qualification, never a claim of novelty; confidence measures the stated argument, not historical attribution. Confidence statements accompanying a different kind identify an editorial calculation inside that note. The symbols \(i\) and \(J\) in the analysis distinguish the late normalized invariant from the conventional elliptic j-invariant; this convention applies only to these notes. Unless a note specifies otherwise, the explicit anharmonic/cyclotomic calculations are made over bases with 6 invertible, as the manuscript eventually requires.

notes.section: 1. The zero divisor, pole filtration, and Weierstrass coordinates
notes.title: The divisor convention and the Lie line
notes.body: The prose about “multiples” of the zero divisor sits beside a section \(1:\mathcal O_C\to\underline L\), positive pole spaces, and \(s^*\underline L\simeq\operatorname{Lie}(C/S)\), so the working convention behaves as \(\mathcal O_C(D)\), not as the ideal \(\mathcal O_C(-D)\). The normal-bundle identity explains that convention: \(s^*\mathcal O_C(D)=N_{D/C}\simeq s^*T_{C/S}\), whereas invariant differentials give its dual. This is an interpretative consistency question, not a proposed replacement of “multiples” in the frozen text.
notes.context: T, cote 54, scan 3, distinguishes the tangent line from invariant differentials; N, D01–D02, already flags variance in universal extensions; cote 62 adds an explicit divisor realization, with a possible sign-convention ambiguity.
notes.register: WG2 §1.1 #3 (unchecked placement question): additional elliptic/Picard material.

notes.section: 1. The zero divisor, pole filtration, and Weierstrass coordinates
notes.title: Riemann–Roch needs the relative base-change step
notes.quote: “on est ramené au cas”; “pour n=0 elle est connue par ailleurs”.
notes.body: For a degree-\(n\) line bundle on a genus-one fibre, Riemann–Roch and duality give \(h^0=n,h^1=0\) when \(n>0\), \(h^0=0,h^1=-n\) when \(n<0\), and the trivial bundle has \(h^0=h^1=1\). The passage from these fibre calculations to locally free direct images and arbitrary base change uses the relative theorem, with the degree-zero trivial-bundle case separately justified, as the manuscript itself indicates. A modern framework is the perfect complex computing proper flat cohomology and its base changes (Stacks Project, n.d., Tag 0A1G); fibre dimensions alone should not be substituted for that argument over a nonreduced base.
notes.context: T, cote 47, scans 7–8, also uses cohomological base change, but for the particular Fourier comparison map; N, F7–F8, leaves its unit-fibre compatibility open; this simpler positive-degree calculation supplies no missing kernel computation.
notes.register: WG2 §2.4 #4: a related method, not a completed Fourier witness.

notes.section: 1. The zero divisor, pole filtration, and Weierstrass coordinates
notes.title: The omitted length-two separation argument
notes.quote: “un raisonnement connu n'utilisant que RR donne le résultat”.
notes.body: The missing very-ampleness argument is to test every length-two subscheme \(Z\) of a geometric fibre: for \(n\geq3\), the line bundle \(\mathcal O_C(nD)(-Z)\) has positive degree and hence vanishing \(H^1\), making restriction to \(Z\) surjective. This separates distinct points and tangent directions, and relative base change then supplies the relative embedding; the general degree-\(2g+1\) criterion is recorded in Stacks Project (n.d., Tag 0H2V). The uncertain inequality in the proposition remains a reading question even though this argument identifies the mathematical threshold.
notes.context: No matching pole-divisor very-ampleness proof occurs in T/N/D; T, cote 44, scan 4, has hyperplane-section statements of a different kind.
notes.register: No directly corresponding mathematical result entry in R.

notes.section: 1. The zero divisor, pole filtration, and Weierstrass coordinates
notes.title: Universal injectivity and the exceptional degree one
notes.body: The universal-injectivity assertion requires the cokernels of the inclusions \(\mathcal E_i\subset\mathcal E_j\) to be locally free, obtainable successively from the divisor exact sequences and the degree-positive \(H^1\)-vanishing. Degree one is exceptional because \(\mathcal E_1=\mathcal E_0\), so its associated graded piece is zero rather than a line. The displayed exclusion is mathematically material and should be retained when comparing the multiplication maps with the later intrinsic description.
notes.context: T, cote 44, scan 3, also uses associated graded objects but in an adic-completion problem; N, D07, does not supply the elliptic filtration statement.

notes.section: 1. The zero divisor, pole filtration, and Weierstrass coordinates
notes.title: What does generation by E₃ mean?
notes.body: Taken as a statement about the filtered affine algebra of \(C-D\), generators with poles of orders two and three give the intended conclusion by their leading terms and induction on pole order. Taken literally as generation of the homogeneous section ring by its degree-three piece alone, it cannot generate degrees one and two; that ring instead uses a degree-one section together with weighted degree-two and degree-three generators. The surrounding shift between the filtered colimit and the direct sum of its filtered pieces is therefore a substantive notation question, not a license to rewrite the corollary.
notes.context: T, cote 44, scan 3, distinguishes a graded direct sum from a product completion; N, D07, makes category restrictions consequential; the present ambiguity is between filtered and homogeneous generation, not that completion issue.

This gap is smaller than, and different from, constructing a restricted Lie algebra or a Dieudonné module.

notes.section: 1. The zero divisor, pole filtration, and Weierstrass coordinates
notes.title: The leading-pole calculation and characteristic p
notes.quote: “ssi p est premier à n”; “est nul”.
notes.body: For a local parameter \(z\), an invariant vector field with \(D(z)\) a unit gives \(D(z^{-n})=-nD(z)z^{-n-1}\), which explains exactly the invertibility and vanishing of the induced leading-term map. The vanishing when \(p\mid n\) concerns this associated graded map, not the whole derivative of every function with pole order \(n\), whose lower-order terms can survive. It consequently does not compute a Hasse invariant, a pth-power operator on the Lie line, or the full \(F,V\)-structure.
notes.context: T, cote 54, scan 7, and N, D03–D05, concern Frobenius, Verschiebung, and restricted Lie data; the present calculation adds a concrete characteristic-p example without settling those comparisons.

This supplies a proof obligation, not a proof from the unfinished marginal instruction.

A modern object-level formulation keeps the torsor and its equivariant coefficient map, yielding a quotient stack; the familiar Weierstrass version is \([W/H]\) (Stacks Project, n.d., Tag 072S). The historical \(\mathcal D\)-representability assertion should not be silently equated with a fine moduli scheme for unstructured curves.

notes.title: Weights two and three require no extraction of a root
notes.position: two matrix groups and boxed relation
notes.body: For units satisfying \(\mu^2=\lambda^3\), the parameter \(u=\mu/\lambda\) satisfies \(u^2=\lambda\) and \(u^3=\mu\), exactly as the manuscript displays. Thus the diagonal subgroup is already a copy of \(\mathbf G_m\) over the base, without adjoining a square or cube root. This is the intrinsic source of weights two and three in the normalized coordinates.
notes.context: T, cote 54, scan 3, supplies the tangent line but not these coordinate weights; T, cote 16, scan 52, concerns genuine Kummer root extraction, a different operation.

The group instead fits a filtration with identified associated graded lines, or a description in which the splitting is allowed to vary. The word is retained literally; the ambiguity concerns the precise moduli problem represented by the group.

notes.title: A proper quotient is not an affine-line torsor
notes.quote: “espace principal homogène sous … fibré vectoriel … inversible”.
notes.body: As written, the proper Brauer–Severi quotient cannot itself be a torsor under an additive line bundle: its geometric fibres are projective lines, whereas such torsor fibres are affine lines. The likely mathematical object for that assertion is the complement of the marked section at infinity, which does carry affine-line transition functions with the indicated linear part. This is an explicit proposed qualification of the claim, not a change to the noun phrase in the transcription.

notes.title: Inversion on E₂ without excluding characteristic two
notes.position: live paragraph after the cancelled opening
notes.quote: “c'est ainsi … sans … la condition … on le verra” [wording uncertain].
notes.body: The forward claim is that inversion acts trivially on the functions with poles of order at most two even without inverting two. In a general Weierstrass equation the pole-two coordinate is fixed by inversion, while the pole-three coordinate transforms by its negative plus lower terms, which supplies the expected characteristic-free verification. The parenthetical reading uncertainty is retained, and the promised verification is not written out on this page.

notes.section: 1. The zero divisor, pole filtration, and Weierstrass coordinates
notes.title: The displayed group retains a central double cover of the affine group
notes.quote: “Ce n'est autre que le groupe affine à 1 variable”.
notes.body: The displayed matrices with diagonal \((1,\lambda^2,\lambda^3)\) project to the affine transformations of the pole-two coordinate, but the projection has kernel \(\{\operatorname{diag}(1,1,\pm1)\}\simeq\mu_2\). Thus, when two is invertible, the written group is a central double cover of the usual affine group, with torus weight two up to inversion, rather than that affine group itself; its nontrivial center distinguishes them. Passing to the quotient action on the genus-zero curve removes this kernel, exactly the deck involution whose information is lost in C16.
notes.context: T, cote 47, scans 4–6, retains inversion as a genuine abelian automorphism; T, cote 54, scan 3, retains the full group object; no same matrix-group identification occurs in T/N/D.

notes.section: 2. Cubic discriminants, cross-ratios, and the S₃ quotient
notes.title: The reducedness qualification in the Kummer scratch work
notes.body: The notes explicitly restrict the passage from \(b^3=0\) or \(c^2=0\) to the vanishing of \(b\) or \(c\) by mentioning the absence of nilpotents. For injectivity, if \(H'_1\cap G=H'_2\cap G\), every \(x\in H'_2\) has a positive multiple in \(G\), hence in \(H'_1\), and convexity forces \(x\in H'_1\); this avoids relying on the unelaborated claim that the quotient embeds in \(G'/G\). The printed question is about extracting and presenting that lemma, not an indication that the final rank statement is false.

notes.title: Discreteness requires the finite-extension hypothesis
notes.quote: “Supposons que L soit une extension finie de K”.
notes.body: Finite index in the value group makes a finite extension of a discrete rank-one valuation discrete, as the typescript proves. This should not be extrapolated to arbitrary algebraic extensions: adjoining all compatible roots of a uniformizer can make the value group nondiscrete, such as \(\mathbf Q\), while retaining rank one. The explicit finite-extension hypothesis therefore distinguishes discreteness from the preceding rank-invariance statement.

notes.quote: “les éléments x_i y_α sont linéairement indépendants”.
notes.body: Choosing representatives of distinct value-group cosets and independent residue classes gives linearly independent products by isolating the terms of minimum valuation and reducing their normalized sum. This proves \(ef\leq[L:K]\) for one extension valuation, matching the modern formulation in Stacks Project (n.d., Tag 0ASH). notes.section: 5. The direct Oda comparison and the two planning questions

notes.body: For an elliptic scheme, the line called Lie here is dual to the invariant-differential line, and in relative dimension one it is also its own determinant line as a rank-one bundle. Such a convention check is logically prior to, and insufficient for, proving compatibility of the actual derived comparison map.
